issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness. Ambulances and pregnancy/birth reminders could fit certain illness contexts, but physical affection as a trigger is hard to reconcile without any supporting illness-related memory or appraisal content, and the three triggers together do not suggest a single coherent illness narrative.

Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/ambient danger vigilance (needing back to wall, reacting to sudden movements, constant environmental scanning), which reads more like fear of assault or attack than threat linked to life-threatening illness. With the given trauma type, this pattern is hard to explain unless supported by corresponding trauma content, which is absent.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport does not match the rest of the profile. No trigger, threat, or memory item suggests transport-related trauma cues or a reason this strategy would be central for this illness-based PTSD presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Rage on recall is not impossible, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the memory content and the illness trauma type. The memories are otherwise characterized by somatic/nonverbal reliving, while the threat pattern is hypervigilance to external attack; intense rage does not help unify these elements into one coherent formulation.

For a trauma type of life-threatening illness, ambulances and hospital smells are plausible triggers, but pregnancy/childbirth reminders are hard to reconcile unless the illness was specifically pregnancy-related; as presented, this trigger set does not describe a coherent illness-linked cue pattern.

It looks like a strategy aimed at a symptom context not otherwise represented.

issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by hypervigilance to interpersonal/physical attack cues (needing back to wall, reacting to others' sudden movements, scanning the room), which fits assault/combat-type danger more than illness-related trauma.

issues.explanation: These threat items do not connect plausibly to the listed illness-related triggers (hospital smell, needles/medical equipment); the cross-node pattern mixes medical trauma cues with a separate attack-style threat state.

issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall is not well supported by the other selected items or the trauma type; the surrounding profile reflects fear, bodily re-experiencing, and medical triggers rather than anger-focused meaning or appraisals.

vignette:
Marta Kowalski is a 41-year-old Polish-American woman who has served as a firefighter for sixteen years. She presents for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 68, referred by her department's employee assistance program after colleagues noticed significant changes in her functioning over the past year.

Fourteen months ago, Marta was admitted to the emergency department following a sudden cardiac event during a routine training exercise. What began as chest tightness became, within minutes, a full arrest. She was resuscitated on the gymnasium floor by her own crewmates, then rushed to hospital where she spent eleven days in the cardiac intensive care unit. During that time she was intubated, connected to multiple drip lines, and subjected to repeated procedures - echocardiograms, catheterisations, blood draws that came so frequently she lost count. She recalled lying immobile under fluorescent lights, unable to speak around the ventilator tube, watching the IV lines run into her arms and feeling entirely disconnected from her own body, as though she were watching someone else be worked on. The smell of the unit - that particular antiseptic sharpness, somewhere between bleach and plastic - was constant. She could not escape it. When she was finally extubated, her first coherent thought was that she had been certain she would not survive.

In the weeks following her discharge, Marta found that the experience resisted being shaped into any kind of story she could tell. When her husband, Darek, asked her what it had been like, she would open her mouth and find nothing - not silence exactly, but an absence of language, as though the event existed in a register that words could not reach. What did come back were physical things: a sudden heaviness in her arms, a constriction across her chest, her body arranging itself into the flat, helpless position she had occupied in that hospital bed. These returns arrived without warning and brought with them the same terror she had felt under those lights - not a memory of terror, but terror itself, present and total.

By autumn she had quietly reorganised her life around avoidance of anything that might open that door. She declined a routine follow-up cardiology appointment, then a second one, telling Darek the scheduling was difficult. She began driving longer routes to avoid passing the hospital where she had been treated. At the station, she had always been the crew member who coordinated with paramedics on scene, but she found she could no longer stand near the ambulance bay - the antiseptic smell that clung to the rigs, the glimpse of an IV bag through open doors, was enough to produce a physical reaction so immediate and overwhelming that she would have to step away and focus hard on something else, deliberately redirecting her attention until the sensation passed. Over time she stopped volunteering for medical-assist calls altogether, citing administrative reasons. Her lieutenant has not yet questioned this directly, but the pattern has not gone unnoticed, and Marta is aware that her credibility within the crew is quietly eroding.

At home she has become difficult to reach emotionally. She had come to believe, without quite articulating it to herself, that allowing any strong feeling to surface risked losing control entirely - that the feelings connected to the illness were too large to be contained once started. So she keeps the emotional temperature low, deflecting Darek's attempts at closeness with practicality and task-focus. He has told her he feels shut out. She does not disagree, but she does not know how to explain what she is managing.

Throughout her days - at the station, at the grocery store, in her own kitchen - Marta moves with a vigilance that exhausts her. She scans rooms without meaning to, tracking exits and anomalies, her body held in a low-grade readiness that never fully releases. She does not feel safe in her own physiology anymore, and that is perhaps the most frightening thing: that the danger, when it came, had been internal.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last month when she froze entirely during a structure fire - not from fear of the fire, but because the medic on scene uncapped a syringe nearby. She stood in full gear, unable to move, for several seconds. She has not told anyone what stopped her. She comes to treatment hoping, above everything, to be able to do her job again - and afraid that what happened to her body once might mean she can no longer trust it.
